subject: Chemistry
title: The Chemistry of Swimming Pools
description: A 60-second lesson on The Chemistry of Swimming Pools.

hook.text: That 'chlorine smell' at pools isn't chlorine. It's chloramines—formed when chlorine reacts with sweat and urine.

buildup.text: Pools add sodium hypochlorite to kill bacteria. The active agent is hypochlorous acid (HOCl).

discovery.text: HOCl penetrates bacterial cell walls and destroys their enzymes. It's incredibly effective at tiny concentrations.

twist.text: When HOCl reacts with ammonia from swimmers' bodies, it forms chloramines—the irritating, smelly compounds.

climax.text: Red eyes at the pool aren't from too much chlorine. They're from too many chloramines—meaning the water is dirty.

punchline.text: The pool smell means dirty, not clean. Real chlorine is odorless in water.

quiz.question: What causes the strong 'chlorine smell' at swimming pools?
options: Chloramines formed when chlorine reacts with sweat and urine
Excess chlorine evaporating from the water
Algae being killed by the chlorine

details.summary: Swimming pools use chlorine-based chemicals like sodium hypochlorite or calcium hypochlorite to sanitize water. In water, these compounds form hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria and algae by oxidizing their cell membranes..
details.whyItMatters: Pool chemistry combines disinfection, pH buffering, and oxidation chemistry to create safe recreational water. It is a practical application of chemical equilibrium principles.
takeaways: Hypochlorous acid is the active disinfectant form of pool chlorine
pH must stay between 7.2 and 7.8 for chlorine to be effective
Chloramines, not chlorine itself, cause the classic pool smell

faq.question: Why do pools smell more strongly of chlorine when they are dirtier?
faq.answer: The strong smell is actually chloramines, formed when hypochlorous acid reacts with nitrogen compounds from sweat, urine, and skin oils. A well-maintained pool has little chloramine and barely smells. The stronger the smell, the more contaminants have reacted with the chlorine.

faq.question: Why does pool pH need to stay within such a narrow range?
faq.answer: Below pH 7.2, water becomes corrosive to metal fixtures and irritating to skin. Above 7.8, hypochlorous acid converts to hypochlorite ion, which is about 100 times less effective as a disinfectant. The narrow range balances chlorine effectiveness, swimmer comfort, and equipment protection.
